newsitem.title: USA: House turns back campaign fund-raising measure.
newsitem.headline: House turns back campaign fund-raising measure.

text.p: In a stunning rebuke to House Republican leaders, lawmakers on Thursday blocked a bill to provide millions of dollars for a wide-ranging investigation of White House fund-raising problems.

Charging that Speaker Newt Gingrich had backed away from promises to cut taxes and balance the budget, 11 Republicans voted against a procedural motion needed to bring a committee funding bill to the floor. It was defeated 213-210.

Lawmakers said they voted against the bill not out of discomfort with the investigation, but because it boosted spending for congressional committees by 14 percent at a time when they are stymied in efforts to eliminate the deficit.

After hours of closed-door meetings, Republican leaders agreed to bring a new bill to the floor on Friday that would freeze most committee funding for 30 days, but still provide the proposed $3.8 million for the White House investigation.

"After backing down on what supposedly was the centrepiece of the Contract with America, the tax cuts, we just said enough is enough," said Florida Republican Joe Scarborough, who complained top Republicans were "battered and confused."
Scarborough said House leaders attempted to "intimidate" the dissidents by forcing them to march to the front of the closed caucus room and explain their vote.
Democrats were unified in opposition to the bill.
The legislation would have allocated funding for House committees during this session of Congress.
It included a 50 percent increase in funds for the Government Reform and Oversight Committee, which is spearheading the investigation of possible Democratic fund-raising abuses in the 1996 campaign.

The bill to be brought up on Friday will freeze funding for all committees for 30 days, except Government Reform. It includes $3.8 million originally earmarked for the investigation along with a separate $8 million fund the committee could dip into if needed, Republican leaders said.
Democrats charge the investigation could total $12-15 million, due in part to what they call the $8 million slush fund.

They charge that Republicans are mounting a partisan witch hunt into White House fundraising problems such as improper donations from foreign interests -- while ignoring congressional fund-raising abuses.

"Today the majority is crossing the line. They are trying to jam a funding bill through ... and they are authorising an investigation that is limited to Democrats," said California Democratic Representative Henry Waxman. "That can't be interpreted as anything other than a coverup."
Government Reform Committee Chairman Dan Burton, a conservative Indiana Republican, has been accused by Democrats of running the panel with a heavy hand and issuing subpoenas without consultations.
Burton became embroiled in a fund-raising controversy of his own this week, when a former lobbyist for Pakistan accused Burton of shaking him down for donations.
"I haven't heard anybody in the conference say the reason for the vote was the investigation or the fact I was a bad guy," Burton told reporters.
Some Republican moderates want his investigation widened, but they stuck with the leadership on the vote.
The brouhaha is the latest in a host of problems that have beset Republicans as they prepare to investigate Democratic fundraising.
Senate Republican leaders were also rebuffed in their initial efforts to secure funding for an investigation.
A Senate committee has launched its own $4.3 million investigation of possible campaign fundraising problems.

Florida Republican Representative Porter Goss said the defeat was "Pretty much a money issue. I don't think it is a big setback at all for the leaders, it was a procedural vote with a lot of issues intertwined in it."
Asked if some Republicans were concerned about Burton's leadership, he said there may be some members who question him, in what he said were "cloakroom whispers."
